5. The prosecution examined seven P.Ws including the victim, doctor and investigating officer who were duly cross-examined by the defence. After close of the prosecution witnesses, the accused on dock were examinee under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to which- they repeated their innocence. The defence did not adduce any evidence. 

 7. The learned Trial Court thereafter it consideration of the evidence on record well as facts and circumstances of the case, however, found the accused-appellants guilty for the offence charged and as such convicted them thereunder and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for the terms as well as ordered to pay a fine with default clause as mentioned above. The accused-appellants being aggrieved and dissatisfied thereby have come up with the present appeal which is opposed by the respondent-State through the learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Md. Rabiu Karim. 

 8. Mr. S. N. Goswami, the learned Advocate for the appellants, took us through the F.l R, charge-sheet, charge so framed, deposition of the prosecution witnesses, impugned judgment and other material papers document as available in paper-book and submits that this ,is  a case of no evidence, but the learned Trial Court arrived at a decision on guess an surmise. He further submits that the prosecution, failed to come . with an independent and disinterested witnesses to prove the occurrence in as much as the, evidence so adduced in order to prove the same is wholly contrary and that the occurrence though allegedly took place at 7/: P.M., the means of  recognition appears to have not been proved in this case and that the alleged injuries sustained by the victim in no way comes under the mischief of Sections 9 (kha) and (ga) of the said Ain, though at best may be treated as simple injuries sustained during scuffle. Accordingly, he submits that the impugned judgment and order of conviction is not sustainable in law. 

 (2) one penetrating injury on lower part of right side of chest wall measuring He proved the medical certificate and his signature thereto issued on this behalf by him Exts-5 series. In cross he failed to re-collect as to whether the victim was at all admitted into hospital. He denied the defence suggestion that he issued the false certificate. This is all about the evidence on record. 

 17. Admittedly, the victim was married with one of the accused of this case, but the marriage tie did not subsist inasmuch as it was ended on 'khola talaq'. It further appears from the evidence of private P.Ws. that all are admittedly close relations of the informant of this case. Against some of whom the accused filed criminal cases, In view of the plain reading of the evidence on record it is crystal clear that sweet relationship does not exist with the parties, but for the reason best known to the prosecution did not come with any independent/disinterested witnesses in order to prove the occurrence which allegedly took place within the vicinity of their house inasmuch as none of the close door neighbours has come to support the prosecution case nor the prosecution felt it necessary to come with any explanation for their absence. In view of 

 such admitted enmity between the parties the evidence of close relations should be swallowed with a grain of salt. Furthermore. all the private P.Ws. found to have said that they were examined by the Daroga 2/3 days after the occurrence, but fact remains that the informant of this case filed a petition case before Sessions Judge, Sherpur, on 2.9.1997 for the occurrence which allegedly took place on 30.7.1997 who sent it to local police station for starting proper case after investigation. In view of such facts and circumstances the examination of some of the witnesses under Section '161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or in other capacity makes a reasonable man suspicious about the bonafide of the prosecution case. 

 18. The investigating officer- P. W. 6 found to have admitted that informant of the present case made a G. D. entry over the self same occurrence on 31.7.1979 i. e. on the following day of occurrence, but for the reason best known to the prosecution has failed to come with the said G.D. entry. An F. I. R. is an accusation. An information relating to the commission of cognizable offence reported to the police by any person with the object of putting the law enforcing agency in motion and such information may come from more than one source and more than one such information may be received by police, but the earliest in point of time disclosing a cognizable offence shall be recorded as an F. 1. R. Once police had. acted and proceeded to investigate on the basis of one particular report disclosing a cognizable offence or other 'information received by police regarding the same offence subsequently shall be nothing, but information received or statement received by police in course of investigation which would not be admissible in evidence under Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that would also not be regarded as the F. I. R. In the instant case from our aforesaid observation it appears that the present informant lodge a G. D. entry over the self-same occurrence on the following date, but the same has not been brought on record to show the bonafide of the prosecution case which ought to have been treated as F. I. R. and the present F. I. R. so lodged by the informant of this case is not F. 1. R. in as much as the same having been recorded long after 

 20. Lastly, in view of admitted bitter relationship between the parties as well as the private witnesses so examined in this case it was desirable for the prosecution to examine the closet' independent and disinterested neighbours. In the face of clear admission that 40/50 co-villagers were present just after the occurrence and they having not been produced in Court to show the bonafide of the prosecution, we find no other alternative but to hold that had they been examined, would not have supported the prosecution case and in view of this matter the benefit of Section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. should go in favour of the defence.
